We report on a 62-year old woman diagnosed with Type 2
diabetes for 24 years and treated with insulin for 13 years.
She was diagnosed with Stiff-Person syndrome (SPS) after
a 5-year history of increasing stiffness and diffuse muscular
pain. The serum and cerebrospinal fluid were negative for the
presence of GAD antibodies. It has been previously shown that
GAD antibodies are present in about 60 percent of patients
with SPS [1,2]. While both GAD antibodies and IA2 are typical
markers for Type 1 diabetes, an association of SPS with Type
1 diabetes is frequently observed and reported in about 25%
of cases [1,3]. Our patient was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes
at age 38 and oral antidiabetic treatment was sufficient over 11
years. In this case, diabetes mellitus and SPS are probably
coincidental and not immunologically associated. Diagnosis
of SPS in our patient was confirmed by clinical measures
and typical electromyographic activation; the latter of which
improved after application of intrathecal instillation of the
muscle relaxant baclofen. The patient was severely restricted
in her ability to move, as the stiffness of the lower extremities
had spread from the thighs to the upper abdomen. In addition,
superimposed episodic muscle spasms in the upper and lower
axial muscles spread to the distal extremities, predominantly
following brisk movement or emotional upset. As oral medica-
tion with benzodiazepine and baclofen did not improve muscle
stiffness and left the patient wheel-chair bound, continuous
intrathecal baclofen treatment by use of an implanted pump
was chosen as a treatment option. Since administration of the
latter therapy, the patient is again mobile with crutches and
her general situation has improved markedly.
Since the initial diagnosis of SPS, the insulin dose had to
be steadily increased to keep the patient’s HbA

1c

levels in an
acceptable range. The insulin analogue mixture (50/50 before
morning and lunch, 25/75 before dinner) used was increased
from 78 IU per day in 2001 to 145 IU/day in 2006. During this
period, patient’s HbA

1c

rose from 6.9% to 8.3%, the BMI
rose from 20 kg/m

2

to 22 kg/m

2

, and her body weight increased
by 5 kg.
The patient was introduced to a continuous, subcutaneous
insulin infusion (CSII) via an insulin pump to stabilize the
diabetes while reducing the relatively high daily insulin dose.
The patient was started on insulin lispro with a basal rate of
60 IU per 24 h and a bolus rate of 3 IU per 12 g carbohydrate
intake. After careful instruction on pump usage and despite a
normal function in vitro, the pump gave recurrent catheter
blockage alarms. The changing of catheters and usage of
another pump did not prevent the alarms from sounding. We
then realized that a blockage alarm was only given by the
pump when the total dosage applied was greater than 4 IU per
delivery. A normal pump function was achieved when the
bolus rates were divided into lower amounts of insulin units
per delivery and by using a needle no longer than 8 mm. Muscle
tension, stiffness and the additional induration of cutaneous
and subcutaneous tissue did not allow for a higher amount of
insulin to be applied per delivery.
Meanwhile, the patient is on 53 IU per 24 h and 2–3 IU per
bread unit, which makes a daily insulin dosage of about 70 IU.
Her HbA

1c

decreased again to 6.9%, and a recent follow-up
showed an HbA

1c

of 6.5%.
Dermal stiffness and tension due to SPS or similar conditions
presumably cause scars, and tissue alterations resulting from
frequent subcutaneous injections over many years may con-
tribute to impaired insulin delivery via the subcutaneous route.
These problems have to be taken into consideration when
using insulin pumps. As a possible solution against catheter
problems and dysfunction, we recommend this approach of
applying very small doses of insulin at a time. Thus, the insulin
resistance in our patient with SPS seems to be predominantly
related to the injection site. This fact should also be considered
part of the problem in SPS patients with Type 1 diabetes, the
presence of high GAD antibodies, and suspected immunological
insulin resistance.
